children: designed its new Arc blockchain for a world in which machines, not people, do most of the transacting, CEO Jeremy Allaire argued in a conversation published Saturday by a16z crypto.
Allaire spoke with a16z crypto founder Chris Dixon and Robert Hackett after Arc, the blockchain Circle built following the success of its USDC

stablecoin, recently reached mainnet. The original idea behind USDC, he recalled, was “an HTTP for money”, a protocol for dollars on the internet that works on any blockchain. As stablecoins grew beyond speculation into payments, regulators began telling institutions that any network they used would have to meet certain standards, and Circle found none built for the purpose. Arc was designed to meet them, with the aim of earning the trust of central banks.

The standards apply to the people running the network. Anyone operating an Arc validator must meet high requirements for operations, information security and compliance, which Allaire credited for the network’s ability to settle transactions with certainty in a fraction of a second. A group of global capital markets, asset management and payments firms and banks has signed on as infrastructure stakeholders, he added, and he hopes every major economic bloc will eventually run a piece of the network.
Circle’s advantages, according to Allaire, start with USDC’s scale. He claimed Circle mints and redeems $150 billion of the coin each quarter, and that deep liquidity on Binance, Coinbase

makes the token capital-efficient. The company’s Cross-Chain Transfer Protocol, which he called the most widely used interoperability tool across blockchains, will also carry assets issued on Arc, such as tokenized equities and credit products. Even so, he does not expect Circle to dominate. The stablecoin market will be “winner-take-most,” he predicted, leaving room for several networks as it grows from hundreds of billions of dollars toward trillions. Among blockchains, he conceded, “no one has a moat.”

AI, Allaire believes, will open new territory. He envisions new types of credit in which people and machines both supply and demand money, in marketplaces that resemble a search advertising exchange more than a bond sale. Early experiments on Arc hint at the range: Fly Brain, a project that turns the rules of fly neurology into 16 megabytes of code, and a planned arbitration system for disputes when one AI hires another.

Dixon cast blockchains as a counterweight to AI’s tendency to favor companies with the most capital, arguing that open networks offer a level playing field with low fees and global access. He called it plausible that most internet participants will eventually be machines.

Pressed on what the financial system will look like in five years, Allaire declined to predict, citing the pace of technological change. He expects machines to handle much of the world’s creative and cognitive work, leaving an economy that produces far more goods and services.

title: Circle CEO Sees AI Agents as Main Users of New Arc Blockchain
